title: Inactivating mutations in NPC1L1 and protection from coronary heart disease
authors: Myocardial Infarction Genetics Consortium Investigators, Stitziel NO, Won HH, Morrison AC, Peloso GM, Do R, et al.
population: Participants of European, African or South Asian ancestry in 16 case-control and cohort studies: 22,092 sequenced and 91,002 genotyped for p.Arg406X
funder: NHLBI grants K08HL114642, T32HL007208, R01HL107816, RC2HL102926 and RC2HL102925; NHGRI grant 5U54HG003067-11; the Foundation for Barnes-Jewish Hospital; a Banting Fellowship from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research; a grant from the Donovan Family Foundation, an investigator-initiated research grant from Merck and a grant from Fondation Leducq (all to S. Kathiresan). Funders of the contributing studies are listed in the Supplementary Appendix.
authorConflicts: Disclosure forms are available with the full text at NEJM.org; not read.
result: Sequencing of NPC1L1 in 7364 patients with coronary heart disease and 14,728 controls identified 15 inactivating mutations; about 1 in 650 persons was a heterozygous carrier. Carriers had LDL cholesterol 12 mg/dl (0.31 mmol/l) lower than non-carriers (P = 0.04) and a 53% lower risk of coronary heart disease (odds ratio 0.47, 95% CI 0.25 to 0.87). Overall, 11 of 29,954 patients (0.04%) and 71 of 83,140 controls (0.09%) carried an inactivating mutation. The study states that ezetimibe lowers LDL cholesterol by inhibiting NPC1L1.
